findings.claim: Flashcard answer: 'Endothermic, releasing the same amount of energy as absorbed.'
findings.truth: An endothermic reaction takes energy in; it does not release it. The reverse reaction absorbs the same amount of energy that the exothermic forward reaction gives out. As written the card teaches the exothermic/endothermic misconception directly.
findings.evidence: spec 5.6.2.2: 'If a reversible reaction is exothermic in one direction, it is endothermic in the opposite direction. The same amount of energy is transferred in each case.'

findings.claim: A Haber process section (equation, 450 degC, 200 atm, iron catalyst), one knowledge check on the Haber catalyst, one practice question on the 450 degC compromise and four flashcards, all presented as examinable.
findings.truth: The Haber process is not in the Trilogy spec: 'Haber' returns no match anywhere in it. Trilogy 5.6.2 ends at the effect of pressure on equilibrium. The chemistry is correct (N2 + 3H2 balances; 450 degC, 200 atm and iron are the standard figures), so the box is kept and labelled rather than deleted. Tom to decide whether to retire the Haber material or leave it labelled.
findings.evidence: spec 5.6.2.1-5.6.2.7; grep 'Haber' over the spec returns nothing

findings.claim: Le Chatelier content is wrapped in a higher-only block in the article, but three knowledge checks (temperature direction, pressure and moles, the change/effect match), two practice questions and four flashcards on the same Higher-only material carry no tier flag.
findings.truth: Spec 5.6.2.4 to 5.6.2.7 (effect of changing conditions, of concentration, of temperature and of pressure on equilibrium) are all headed (HT only). The lesson tier is 'both', so Foundation students meet Higher-only equilibrium work in the questions with no warning. Options: mark those items Higher-only in the question data, split the lesson, or accept the over-teach. Cannot be settled from lesson metadata alone. Recommendation: flag the items, do not split the lesson.

findings.claim: A whole lesson on alkene addition reactions, alcohols, carboxylic acids and esters inside a Combined Science Chemistry Paper 2 unit, with no scope label.
findings.truth: Trilogy organic chemistry (5.7) stops at crude oil, alkanes, fractional distillation, combustion, cracking and 'alkenes react with bromine water', and states that students do not need the names or formulae of individual alkenes. Alcohols, carboxylic acids, esters, hydrogenation, hydration and fermentation are separate Chemistry only. Every fact and equation in the lesson checks out (C2H5OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O balances; 2C2H5OH + 2Na -> 2C2H5ONa + H2 balances; 2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 balances; the esterification balances; Mr of C3H6 = 36 + 6 = 42; dichromate orange to green; fermentation 25-30 degC; hydration 300 degC, 60-70 atm, phosphoric acid), so the content is kept and labelled.
findings.evidence: spec 5.7.1.1-5.7.1.4; grep 'carboxylic' returns nothing and 'alcohol' hits only biology lifestyle statements

findings.claim: 'If asked to write the formula of an ester, remember the pattern: acid name first + alcohol name (e.g. ethanoic acid + methanol = methyl ethanoate).'
findings.truth: The rule contradicts its own example. In an ester name the alcohol supplies the first part (methyl) and the acid supplies the second (ethanoate). A student following the stated rule would write the name backwards.
findings.evidence: settled naming convention: methyl ethanoate = methanol + ethanoic acid

findings.claim: A whole lesson on addition polymerisation, condensation polymerisation, atom economy and natural polymers inside a Combined Science unit. The opening line says 'For separate chemistry, you need to understand two types', which is not a clear scope warning.
findings.truth: Trilogy 5.7 contains one sentence on polymers ('alkenes are used to produce polymers'); there is no polymerisation statement, no condensation polymers, no natural polymers and no atom economy anywhere in the spec. All the chemistry is correct (100 percent atom economy for addition; PET, nylon, peptide and phosphodiester links; starch and cellulose from glucose), so the content is kept and labelled.
findings.evidence: spec 5.7.1.4; grep 'condensation polymer' and 'atom economy' over the spec returns nothing

findings.claim: Mark scheme for the polyester repeating-unit calculation: 'Mr of acid + Mr of diol minus Mr of water lost = 130 + 62 - 18 = 174'.
findings.truth: A dicarboxylic acid and a diol join at both ends, so a polyester repeating unit loses TWO water molecules, not one. The answer is 130 + 62 - 36 = 156. Check against PET: terephthalic acid 166 plus ethane-1,2-diol 62 = 228, and the PET repeat unit is 192, a loss of 36.

findings.claim: A lesson on flame tests, metal hydroxide precipitates, carbonate, halide and sulfate tests and instrumental analysis inside a Combined Science unit. Only a passing 'In separate chemistry' phrase flags it.
findings.truth: Trilogy 5.8.2 lists only four tests: hydrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide and chlorine. Flame tests, flame emission spectroscopy and metal hydroxide precipitates return no match. Those four gas tests are in scope, but they already appear in lesson 4 of this unit, so the only examinable part of lesson 10 is a duplicate. Every test result in the lesson is correct (Li crimson, Na yellow, K lilac, Ca orange-red, Cu green; Cu2+ blue, Fe2+ green, Fe3+ brown, Al3+ white dissolving in excess; AgCl white, AgBr cream, AgI yellow; BaSO4 white), so the content is kept and labelled.
findings.evidence: spec 5.8.1-5.8.2.4; grep 'flame test' and 'flame emission' over the spec returns nothing

findings.claim: A whole lesson on corrosion, named alloys, the Haber process and NPK fertilisers inside a Combined Science unit, with no scope label.
findings.truth: 'corrosion', 'rusting', 'Haber' and 'NPK' all return no match in the Trilogy spec. Trilogy alloys sit in 5.2.2.7, which is Chemistry Paper 1 not Paper 2, and go no further than 'pure metals are too soft, alloys are harder', with no named alloys. The chemistry is correct (rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide; zinc gives sacrificial protection; bronze copper+tin, brass copper+zinc, stainless steel iron+chromium+nickel; NH3 + HNO3 -> NH4NO3 balances; 28 tonnes of N2 gives 34 tonnes of NH3), so the content is kept and labelled.
findings.evidence: spec 5.2.2.7 and 5.10; grep 'Haber', 'NPK', 'corrosion' and 'rusting' over the spec returns nothing

findings.claim: The two Key Fact boxes carry each other's data-revision-tip prompts: the purity box is prompted with 'recall the four gas tests', and the gas-test box is prompted with 'explain why pure substances have sharp melting points'.
findings.truth: The two prompts are swapped and should be exchanged. Not edited here because the raw dump truncates both attribute values, so no safe find string could be built. A one-line swap in the editor fixes it.
findings.evidence: lesson 4 content_html, data-revision-tip on the n3 and n12 key-fact blocks

findings.claim: Chromatography is explained only as 'different substances travel different distances depending on their solubility'.
findings.truth: The spec requires the stationary phase and mobile phase idea: separation depends on the distribution of a substance between the two phases, not on solubility alone. An answer that names only solubility can lose the second explanation mark. Worth one added sentence, but nothing in the lesson is false.
findings.evidence: spec 5.8.1.3: 'Chromatography involves a stationary phase and a mobile phase. Separation depends on the distribution of substances between the phases.'

findings.claim: No required practical is named anywhere in this unit.
findings.truth: Chemistry Paper 2 carries three of the qualification's required practicals: 11 (how changes in concentration affect rates, by gas volume and by colour change or turbidity), 12 (paper chromatography and Rf values) and 13 (analysis and purification of water samples, including pH, dissolved solids and distillation). Lessons 1, 4 and 7 teach the science but never name the practical, so students cannot recognise a required-practical question. A coverage gap, not an error.

findings.claim: Ion charges in the takeaways are written as Cu<sup>2</sup>+, Fe<sup>2</sup>+, Fe<sup>3</sup>+ and Cl−.
findings.truth: The charge sign sits outside the superscript, and the halide charges are not superscripted at all, so Cl− renders as a minus sign rather than a chloride ion. Correct notation is Cu<sup>2+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup>. Cosmetic; no mark depends on it.

summary: Eleven lessons checked against the Combined Science: Trilogy spec. Lessons 8, 9, 10 and 11 sit wholly or largely outside the qualification (alcohols, carboxylic acids, esters, condensation and natural polymers, atom economy, flame tests, ion precipitate tests, corrosion, named alloys, the Haber process and NPK fertilisers all return no match in the spec); their chemistry is sound, so each is labelled 'Separate Chemistry only' at the top of the content and in the description rather than deleted. The Haber box inside lesson 2 is labelled the same way. Two hard errors: a lesson 2 flashcard that defines the endothermic reverse reaction as releasing energy, and a lesson 9 polyester calculation that loses one water molecule per repeating unit instead of two. Lesson 8's ester-naming tip contradicted its own example. Every other worked example, equation and answer key recomputed clean, including all 55 knowledge checks.
